title: Counters and group keys
sub: Valid Anagram and Group Anagrams: int[26] instead of a dictionary, a group key and the Unicode trap
cards/0/title: Valid Anagram: the problem and its signals
cards/0/body:
Valid Anagram (LeetCode #242). Given strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s: the same letters in the same quantities, in any order. On LeetCode the length is up to 5·10⁴ and only lowercase English letters appear; the follow-up asks: what if the input contains Unicode characters?

The signal from the previous lesson is the question “how many times?”. An anagram is equality of multisets: “aab” and “abb” are built from the same letters a and b, yet they are not anagrams. So a HashSet (“seen or not”) is not enough here — you need a counter, “character → how many times”.

The first solution that comes to mind is to sort both strings and compare them: anagrams have the same sorted letters. Time is O(k log k) for strings of length k, memory is O(k): two character arrays plus two more strings.
cards/1/q: In which problems is a set not enough, so you need a “how many times” counter? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Can a ransom note be built from the letters of a magazine, each magazine letter used at most once
cards/1/options/1: Does the array contain at least one duplicate
cards/1/options/2: Do two words have the same set of distinct letters
cards/1/options/3: Does every number in the array appear exactly twice
cards/1/options/4: The first non-repeating character of a string
cards/1/explain: The note needs each letter as many times as it appears in the note — that is a quantity, not a fact. “Exactly twice” and “non-repeating” are about quantities too: a counter, and for the first non-repeating character a second pass over the string as well. A duplicate and a set of distinct letters are “seen or not” questions: a HashSet is enough, and it reports the duplicate by itself — Add returns false.
cards/2/title: A counter: int[26] instead of a dictionary
cards/2/body:
A counter in one pass: add 1 for every character of s, subtract 1 for every character of t. Invariant: after the pass, counts[c] = (how many times c occurs in s) − (how many times in t). The strings are anagrams exactly when all counters are zero. Time is O(k) instead of O(k log k).

The key here is a character, and the alphabet is small and dense: 'a'..'z'. Then no hash table is needed — an array indexed by c - 'a' replaces it: 26 counters, 104 bytes, no hashing and no buckets. A Dictionary<char, int> gives the same O(k), but every counts[c]++ is a hash plus two lookups (read and write), and the dictionary itself is an object and two arrays on the heap. On the same strings the array is several times faster.

No heap at all: Span<int> counts = stackalloc int[26] is an array on the method's stack — zero allocations, nothing for the garbage collector to collect. This is the trick from the first unit: no unsafe, and in Unity since 2021.2 (.NET Standard 2.1). The documentation does not guarantee the contents of stackalloc memory, so clear it before counting: counts.Clear(). The price is a set of restrictions: stackalloc memory lives only until the method returns, and the Span itself cannot be stored in a class field or captured in a lambda.

In a game: the same trick works whenever the key is a small dense number: items by (int)ItemType, units by team number — an array instead of a dictionary.
cards/3/q: Assemble Valid Anagram with a counter in a single pass.
cards/3/explain: Different lengths mean false right away; it also allows a single loop over a shared index i. A character of s adds, a character of t subtracts, and the index c − 'a' maps 'a'..'z' to 0..25. Any non-zero counter at the end is a difference in quantity. Without subtracting 'a' the index would be 97..122 — outside an array of 26. c > 0 would also do: with equal lengths the counters sum to 0, so if any is non-zero, some is positive.
cards/4/title: Group Anagrams: invent a group key
cards/4/body:
Group Anagrams (LeetCode #49). Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together: ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"] → [[eat,tea,ate],[tan,nat],[bat]]. Up to 10⁴ strings of length up to 100, lowercase English letters.

Comparing every pair of strings is O(n²·k). Instead, invent a group key: a value that is the same for all anagrams and different for non-anagrams. Then a “key → list of strings” dictionary does the job: each string lands in its bucket with a single lookup. The whole difficulty of the problem is inventing the key.

Key 1 — the sorted letters: “eat”, “tea”, “ate” → “aet”. O(k log k) per string, O(n·k log k) in total. Key 2 — a counter: 26 numbers with a separator, “eat” → “1#0#0#0#1#…”. O(k + 26) per string — better when strings are long. For k ≤ 100 the difference is small, and the sorted key is easier to write without bugs. Memory is O(n·k) either way: the dictionary holds every string and key.

An int[26] itself does not work as a dictionary key: arrays are compared by reference, so every word would get its own group. That is why the counter is turned into a string (or into your own struct with IEquatable).

In a game: this is how objects are grouped for instanced rendering — the key is (Mesh, Material), the value is a list of matrices, and each group is drawn in batches with Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced (Unity 2021.2+; earlier, DrawMeshInstanced), up to 1023 instances per call.
cards/5/task: Step through the trace on [tea, eat, aab, bab, aba, ate]. The rig stops twice and asks where a word goes: decide by the key, not by the set of letters.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Into the “aab” group: same letters, a and b
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: A new group with the key “abb”
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: A new group with the key “bab”
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: The next word is “bab”. Its letters are the same as in “aab”: a and b. Where does it go?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: The key is all the letters, repeats included, in order: “bab” → “abb”. “aab” has two a’s and one b, “bab” has one a and two b’s: they are not anagrams, and the keys differ. A key made of distinct letters ({a, b}) would glue them into one group — a common mistake.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: Now “aba”. What does the code do?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: Sorting gives a canonical form: all permutations of the same letters share one. “aba” → “aab”, that key already exists, TryGetValue hands over the group’s list, and the word is added to it. A new list is created only for a new key.
cards/6/q: A counter key for Group Anagrams. It puts “aaaaaaaaaaab” and “abbbbbbbbbbb” into one group, yet they are not anagrams. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: Without a separator the numbers run together: 11 and 1 give “111”, and so do 1 and 11. The key is no longer unambiguous, and different strings land in one group. The fix is a separator: sb.Append(n).Append('#') — then “11#1#…” and “1#11#…” differ. While every counter is below 10 the bug stays invisible: only words with a letter repeated 10 times or more expose it.
cards/7/body:
The first question to the interviewer: which characters can appear. The solution depends on the answer.

Only a–z — int[26]. But for 'A' the index 'A' - 'a' is −32, for 'é' it is 136: IndexOutOfRangeException. Case is normalized up front, and with ToLowerInvariant(), not ToLower(): the latter depends on the thread’s culture, and in the Turkish locale "I".ToLower() is the dotless “ı”.

Any characters — a counter in a dictionary. But a char in .NET is not a character, it is a UTF-16 code unit: emoji and rare CJK characters take two chars (a surrogate pair). They must be counted as one code point — char.ConvertToUtf32 joins the pair into one number.

Normalization. “é” can be the single character U+00E9 or the pair “e” + U+0301 (a combining accent). They look the same on screen, but the counters differ. Before comparing, bring both strings to one form: s.Normalize() (form NFC by default).

In a game: player names, chat, localization into Japanese or Chinese — exactly the case where int[26] crashes.
cards/8/q: The strings may contain any Unicode characters. What is true? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: int[26] indexed by c - 'a' throws IndexOutOfRangeException on 'A' or 'é'
cards/8/options/1: A Dictionary<char, int> counts an emoji as one character
cards/8/options/2: A single-character “é” and “e” with a combining accent give different counters without Normalize()
cards/8/options/3: ToLower() returns the same result on every machine
cards/8/options/4: char.ConvertToUtf32 turns a surrogate pair into one code point
cards/8/explain: 'A' − 'a' = −32 and 'é' − 'a' = 136 — both indices are outside 0..25. An emoji is two chars, and a dictionary over char counts the two halves separately. The two spellings of “é” differ until normalized. ToLower() uses the thread’s culture: in Turkish “I” becomes “ı”, so keys need ToLowerInvariant(). ConvertToUtf32 is exactly what joins the pair into one code point.
cards/9/title: Variations: the same counter, a different key
cards/9/body:
Ransom Note (#383): can the note be built from the magazine’s letters. Count the magazine’s letters, then subtract the note’s; if a counter goes negative, it cannot. O(m + n), memory O(1).

All anagrams of a pattern in a string (Find All Anagrams, #438): a window of length |p| slides along the string, +1 for the character entering, −1 for the one leaving, and the window’s counter is compared with the pattern’s. The same counter, an O(1) update per step — details are in the sliding window unit.

Shifted strings (Group Shifted Strings, #249): “abc”, “bcd”, “xyz” form one group because neighbouring letters are the same distance apart. The key is the string shifted so that it starts with 'a'. This is the main skill of the lesson: ask what the members of a group have in common, and make that the key.

Long strings, few words (k = 10⁴, n = 100): a counter key in O(k) instead of sorting in O(k log k).
cards/10/q: You solve Group Anagrams out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: which characters, any uppercase, does the group order matter, what are n and the lengths
cards/10/items/1: Name the brute force: compare every pair of strings — O(n²·k)
cards/10/items/2: Idea: anagrams share a key — the sorted letters; a “key → list” dictionary
cards/10/items/3: Write the code while stating: the key is equal for anagrams and different for everything else
cards/10/items/4: Run an example: eat, tea, tan — two groups
cards/10/items/5: State the complexity: O(n·k log k) time, O(n·k) memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: an empty string, a single word, Unicode, long strings — a counter key
cards/10/explain: The statement, the baseline, the key idea, the code, an example, the complexity, edge cases. Ask about Unicode at the very first step — the answer decides whether int[26] and sorting chars are enough.
cards/11/title: The cost of a string key
cards/11/body:
A string key is not free. For every word ToCharArray allocates an array and new string allocates one more string: for 10⁴ words that is 2·10⁴ heap objects. And a lookup by a string key is not “O(1)” but O(k): .NET computes a string’s hash over every character on every call (the string does not store it), and when hashes match, Equals walks the string once more.

The easiest thing to remove is the character array: one buffer for all the words, sort its prefix and build the string from a slice of the buffer. One allocation per word remains — the key itself.
cards/11/deep:
A key without intermediate copies. string.Create(length, state, (span, st) => …) (.NET Core 2.1+, .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2) hands you a Span<char> over the new string’s own memory: copy the letters into it and sort in place. Sorting a Span<T> — MemoryExtensions.Sort — exists only since .NET 5; in Unity sort the buffer with Array.Sort, as above.

A lookup with no string at all (.NET 9+). groups.GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>() searches a Dictionary<string, …> by a ReadOnlySpan<char>: sort the letters in a stackalloc buffer and look up by it. The string key is created only for a new group — when writing through the same lookup. It needs a comparer that can compare a span with a string: the default one for string, StringComparer.Ordinal and OrdinalIgnoreCase can.

String hashing in a dictionary. In modern .NET a Dictionary<string, …> with the default comparer (or with StringComparer.Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase) first hashes strings without randomization — it is faster. If an insert has to walk a chain of more than 100 entries, the dictionary switches to the randomized hash and rehashes everything. The protection against collision attacks stays, and in the normal case it costs nothing.

stackalloc in a loop. stackalloc memory is released only when the method returns. Inside a loop over 10⁴ words every iteration bites off a new chunk of the stack — all the way to a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught (the analyzer warns about it with rule CA2014). Allocate the buffer once before the loop and zero it with counts.Clear() before every word. Code without Clear() usually works: by default the C# compiler asks the runtime to zero a method’s locals (the localsinit flag). But with the [SkipLocalsInit] attribute (.NET 5+) there is no zeroing, and the counters start with leftover stack garbage.

Surrogates and sorting. Sorting by char tears surrogate pairs apart, and a key of sorted UTF-16 code units can glue different strings together: the code point pairs U+1F600 + U+1F900 and U+1F500 + U+1FA00 consist of the same units D83D, D83E, DD00, DE00. For a Unicode key sort code points (int), not chars. .NET Core 3.0+ has System.Text.Rune and s.EnumerateRunes() for this; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no Rune — char.ConvertToUtf32 remains. And a “character” as the player sees it is bigger still — a grapheme cluster (a letter with accents, an emoji with a skin tone modifier); StringInfo.GetTextElementEnumerator walks those.
